{{Short description|Algebraic element satisfying some of the criteria of an inverse}}
{{redirect|Pseudoinverse|the Moore–Penrose inverse, sometimes referred to as "the pseudoinverse"|Moore–Penrose inverse}}
In [[mathematics]], and in particular, [[algebra]], a '''generalized inverse''' (or, '''g-inverse''') of an element ''x'' is an element ''y'' that has some properties of an [[inverse element]] but not necessarily all of them. The purpose of constructing a generalized inverse of a matrix is to obtain a matrix that can serve as an inverse in some sense for a wider class of matrices than [[invertible matrix|invertible matrices]]. Generalized inverses can be defined in any [[mathematical structure]] that involves [[Associative property|associative]] multiplication, that is, in a [[semigroup]].  This article describes generalized inverses of a [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] <math>A</math>.

A matrix <math>A^\mathrm{g} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}</math> is a generalized inverse of a matrix <math>A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}</math> if <math> AA^\mathrm{g}A = A.</math><ref name=":0">{{harvnb|Ben-Israel|Greville|2003|pp=2, 7}}</ref><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> A generalized inverse exists for an arbitrary matrix, and when a matrix has a [[#Motivation|regular inverse]], this inverse is its unique generalized inverse.<ref name=":0" />

== Motivation == <!-- [[Regular inverse]] links here.  Please do not change. -->
Consider the [[System of linear equations|linear system]]

:<math>Ax = y</math>

where <math>A</math> is an <math>m \times n</math> matrix and <math>y \in \mathcal C(A),</math> the [[column space]] of <math>A</math>.  If <math>m = n</math> and <math>A</math> is [[Invertible matrix|nonsingular]] then <math>x = A^{-1}y</math> will be the solution of the system.  Note that, if <math>A</math> is nonsingular, then

:<math>AA^{-1}A = A.</math>

Now suppose <math>A</math> is rectangular (<math>m \neq n</math>), or square and singular. Then we need a right candidate <math>G</math> of order <math>n \times m</math> such that for all <math>y \in \mathcal C(A),</math>

:<math>AGy = y.</math><ref>{{harvnb|Rao|Mitra|1971|p=24}}</ref>

That is, <math>x=Gy</math> is a solution of the linear system <math>Ax = y</math>. 
Equivalently, we need a matrix <math>G</math> of order <math>n\times m</math> such that

:<math>AGA = A.</math>

Hence we can define the '''generalized inverse''' as follows:  Given an <math>m \times n</math> matrix <math>A</math>, an <math>n \times m</math> matrix <math>G</math> is said to be a generalized inverse of <math>A</math> if <math>AGA = A.</math>{{zwj}}<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{harvnb|Nakamura|1991|pp=41–42}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{harvnb|Rao|Mitra|1971|pp=vii, 20}}</ref> The matrix <math>A^{-1}</math> has been termed a '''regular inverse''' of <math>A</math> by some authors.<ref>{{harvnb|Rao|Mitra|1971|pp=19–20}}</ref>

[[File:Generalized inverse subspaces-reflexive.svg|thumb|G (denoted as X in the picture) is a generalized inverse of A, and U and V are the domain and codomain of A respectively.<br>In this case, G maps A's [[Image (mathematics)#Image of a function|image]] (column space, im A) to a complement subspace of its [[Kernel (algebra)|kernel]] (null space, ker A) bijectively, and maps a complement subspace of A's image all to zero.]]

The problem is how to choose an <math>x</math> as the output of <math>G</math> for every <math>y</math> when the map <math>x \mapsto y = Ax</math> is not bijective.

* If <math>A</math> is ''not surjective'', then not all <math>y</math>'s in its [[codomain]] have corresponding <math>x</math>'s via <math>A</math>. To circumvent it, we just let <math>G</math> map those <math>y</math>'s to arbitrary values.

: For example, decompose the codomain of <math>A</math> as the [[direct sum]] of the column space <math>\mathcal C(A)</math> and a complement subspace, and construct <math>G</math> as follows.
:* For <math>y</math>'s in the former subspace, let <math>G</math> map back to the corresponding <math>x</math>'s.
:* For <math>y</math>'s in the latter subspace, let <math>G</math> map them all to zero (as there're no corresponding <math>x</math>'s).
:* For other <math>y</math>'s, decompose them as the sum of the above two components, apply <math>G</math> respectively, then take the sum.

* If <math>A</math> is ''not injective'', then some <math>y</math>'s correspond to multiple <math>x</math>'s via <math>A</math>. To circumvent it, we let <math>G</math> map every <math>y</math> to one of the <math>x</math>'s  according an algorithm.

: For example, decompose the domain of <math>A</math> as the [[direct sum]] of <math>\ker A</math> and a complement subspace. For every possible <math>y</math>, its [[preimage]] must be parallel to <math>\ker A</math> and intersect the chosen complement subspace at a single point. Let <math>G</math> map the <math>y</math> to this point.

* If <math>A</math> is ''neither surjective nor injective'', we combine the above two tricks.

: The picture on the right is an example.

== Types ==
Important types of generalized inverse include:
* One-sided inverse (right inverse or left inverse)
** Right inverse:  If the matrix <math>A</math> has dimensions <math>m \times n</math> and <math> \textrm{rank} (A) = m</math>, then there exists an <math>n \times m</math> matrix <math>A_{\mathrm{R}}^{-1}</math> called the '''right inverse''' of <math>A</math> such that <math> A A_{\mathrm{R}}^{-1} = I_m </math>, where <math>I_m</math> is the <math>m \times m</math> [[identity matrix]].
** Left inverse:  If the matrix <math>A</math> has dimensions <math>m \times n</math> and <math> \textrm{rank} (A) = n</math>, then there exists an <math>n \times m</math> matrix <math>A_{\mathrm{L}}^{-1}</math> called the '''left inverse''' of <math>A</math> such that <math>A_{\mathrm{L}}^{-1} A = I_n </math>, where <math>I_n</math> is the <math>n \times n</math> identity matrix.<ref name=":4" />
* [[Bott–Duffin inverse]]
* [[Drazin inverse]]
* [[Moore–Penrose inverse]]

Some generalized inverses are defined and classified based on the Penrose conditions:

# <math> A A^\mathrm{g} A = A </math>
# <math> A^\mathrm{g} A A^\mathrm{g}= A^\mathrm{g} </math>
# <math> (A A^\mathrm{g})^* = A A^\mathrm{g} </math>
# <math> (A^\mathrm{g} A)^* = A^\mathrm{g} A, </math>

where <math>{}^*</math> denotes [[conjugate transpose]]. If <math>A^\mathrm{g}</math> satisfies the first condition, then it is a '''generalized inverse''' of <math>A</math>. If it satisfies the first two conditions, then it is a '''reflexive generalized inverse''' of <math>A</math>.  If it satisfies all four conditions, then it is the '''pseudoinverse''' of <math>A</math>, which is denoted by <math>A^+</math> and also known as the '''Moore–Penrose inverse''', after the pioneering works by [[E. H. Moore]] and [[Roger Penrose]].<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{harvnb|Rao|Mitra|1971|pp=20, 28, 50–51}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{harvnb|Ben-Israel|Greville|2003|p=7}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Campbell|Meyer|1991|p=10}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|James|1978|p=114}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Nakamura|1991|p=42}}</ref> It is convenient to define an '''<math>I</math>-inverse''' of <math>A</math> as an inverse that satisfies the subset <math>I \subset \{1, 2, 3, 4\}</math> of the Penrose conditions listed above. Relations, such as <math>A^{(1, 4)} A A^{(1, 3)} = A^+</math>, can be established between these different classes of <math>I</math>-inverses.<ref name=":0" />

When <math>A</math> is non-singular, any generalized inverse <math>A^\mathrm{g}</math> is equal to <math>A^{-1}</math> and is therefore unique. For a singular <math>A</math>, some generalized inverses, such as the Drazin inverse and the Moore–Penrose inverse, are unique, while others are not necessarily uniquely defined.

== Examples ==
=== Non-reflexive generalized inverse ===
[[File:Generalized inverse subspaces-general.svg|thumb|G (denoted as X in the picture) is a non-reflexive generalized inverse of A, and U and V are the domain and codomain of A respectively (same below).]]

Let

: <math>A = \begin{bmatrix}
    1 & 0 & 3 \\
    2 & 0 & 6 \\
    0 & 0 & 0
  \end{bmatrix}, \quad 
  G = \begin{bmatrix}
    1 & 0 & 0 \\
    0 & 0 & 1 \\
    0 & 0 & 0
  \end{bmatrix}.
</math>

Obviously, <math>A</math> is singular. <math> A </math> and <math> G </math> satisfy Penrose conditions (1), but not the other there. Hence, <math> G </math> is a non-reflexive generalized inverse of <math> A </math>.

The first column of <math>A</math> spans <math>\operatorname{im} A</math>, and <math>G</math> maps it to <math>(1,0,0)</math>, which does not lie in <math>\ker A</math>. Additionally, <math>G</math> maps <math>(0,0,1)</math> to <math>(0,1,0)</math>, which lies in <math>\ker A</math>. The relationship is summarized in the picture on the right.

=== Reflexive generalized inverse ===
[[File:Generalized inverse subspaces-reflexive.svg|thumb|G (denoted as X in the picture) is a reflexive generalized inverse of A|226x226px]]

Let

: <math>A = \begin{bmatrix}
    1 & 2 & 3 \\
    4 & 5 & 6 \\
    7 & 8 & 9
  \end{bmatrix}, \quad 
  G = \begin{bmatrix}
    -\frac{5}{3} &  \frac{2}{3} & 0 \\[4pt]
     \frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\[4pt]
               0 &            0 & 0
  \end{bmatrix}.
</math>

Since <math>\det(A) = 0</math>, <math> A </math> is singular and has no regular inverse.  However, <math> A </math> and <math> G </math> satisfy Penrose conditions (1) and (2), but not (3) or (4).  Hence, <math> G </math> is a reflexive generalized inverse of <math> A </math>.

=== One-sided inverse ===
Let

: <math>A = \begin{bmatrix}
    1 & 2 & 3 \\
    4 & 5 & 6
  \end{bmatrix}, \quad 
  A_\mathrm{R}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}
    -\frac{17}{18} &  \frac{8}{18} \\[4pt]
    -\frac{2}{18}  &  \frac{2}{18} \\[4pt]
     \frac{13}{18} & -\frac{4}{18}
  \end{bmatrix}.
</math>

Since <math> A </math> is not square, <math> A </math> has no regular inverse.  However, <math> A_\mathrm{R}^{-1} </math> is a right inverse of <math> A </math>.  The matrix <math> A </math> has no left inverse.

<gallery>
File:Generalized inverse subspaces-left.svg|<math>X</math> is a left inverse of <math>A</math><br>(<math>X A = I_U</math>)
File:Generalized inverse subspaces-right.svg|<math>X</math> is a right inverse of <math>A</math><br>(<math>A X = I_V</math>)
</gallery>

=== Inverse of other semigroups (or rings) ===

The element ''b'' is a generalized inverse of an element ''a'' [[if and only if]] <math>a \cdot b \cdot a = a</math>, in any semigroup (or [[ring (mathematics)|ring]], since the [[multiplication]] function in any ring is a semigroup).

The generalized inverses of the element 3 in the ring <math>\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}</math> are 3, 7, and 11, since in the ring <math>\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}</math>:

:<math>3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 = 3</math>
:<math>3 \cdot 7 \cdot 3 = 3</math>
:<math>3 \cdot 11 \cdot 3 = 3</math>

The generalized inverses of the element 4 in the ring <math>\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}</math> are 1, 4, 7, and 10, since in the ring <math>\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}</math>:

:<math>4 \cdot 1 \cdot 4 = 4</math>
:<math>4 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 = 4</math>
:<math>4 \cdot 7 \cdot 4 = 4</math>
:<math>4 \cdot 10 \cdot 4 = 4</math>

If an element ''a'' in a semigroup (or ring) has an inverse, the inverse must be the only generalized inverse of this element, like the elements 1, 5, 7, and 11 in the ring <math>\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}</math>.

In the ring <math>\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}</math> any element is a generalized inverse of 0; however 2 has no generalized inverse, since there is no ''b'' in <math>\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}</math> such that <math>2 \cdot b \cdot 2 = 2</math>.

== Construction ==

The following characterizations are easy to verify:
* A right inverse of a [[square matrix|non-square matrix]] <math>A</math> is given by <math>A_\mathrm{R}^{-1} = A^{\intercal} \left( A A^{\intercal} \right)^{-1}</math>, provided <math>A</math> has full row rank.<ref name=":4">{{harvnb|Rao|Mitra|1971|p=19}}</ref>
* A left inverse of a non-square matrix <math>A</math> is given by <math>A_\mathrm{L}^{-1} = \left(A^{\intercal} A \right)^{-1} A^{\intercal}</math>, provided <math>A</math> has full column rank.<ref name=":4" />
* If <math>A = BC</math> is a [[rank factorization]],  then <math>G = C_\mathrm{R}^{-1} B_\mathrm{L}^{-1}</math> is a g-inverse of <math>A</math>, where <math>C_\mathrm{R}^{-1}</math> is a right inverse of <math>C</math> and <math>B_\mathrm{L}^{-1}</math> is left inverse of <math>B</math>.
* If <math>A = P \begin{bmatrix}I_r & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} Q</math> for any non-singular matrices <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math>, then <math>G = Q^{-1} \begin{bmatrix}I_r & U \\ W & V \end{bmatrix} P^{-1}</math> is a generalized inverse  of <math>A</math> for arbitrary <math>U, V</math> and <math>W</math>.
* Let <math>A</math> be of rank <math>r</math>. [[Without loss of generality]], let<math display="block">A = \begin{bmatrix}B & C\\ D & E\end{bmatrix},</math>where <math>B_{r \times r}</math> is the non-singular submatrix of <math>A</math>. Then,<math display="block">G = \begin{bmatrix} B^{-1} & 0\\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}</math>is a generalized inverse of <math>A</math> if and only if <math>E=DB^{-1}C</math>.

== Uses ==
Any generalized inverse can be used to determine whether a [[system of linear equations]] has any solutions, and if so to give all of them. If any solutions exist for the ''n'' × ''m'' linear system

:<math>Ax = b,</math>

with vector <math>x</math> of unknowns and vector <math>b</math> of constants, all solutions are given by

:<math>x = A^\mathrm{g}b + \left[I - A^\mathrm{g}A\right]w,</math>

parametric on the arbitrary vector <math>w</math>, where <math>A^\mathrm{g}</math> is any generalized inverse of <math>A</math>. Solutions exist if and only if <math>A^\mathrm{g}b</math> is a solution, that is, if and only if <math>AA^\mathrm{g}b = b</math>. If ''A'' has full column rank, the bracketed expression in this equation is the [[zero matrix]] and so the solution is unique.<ref>{{harvnb|James|1978|pp=109–110}}</ref>

== Generalized inverses of matrices ==
The generalized inverses of matrices can be characterized as follows. Let <math>A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}</math>, and

<math display="block">A = U \begin{bmatrix} \Sigma_1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} V^\operatorname{T}</math>

be its [[singular-value decomposition]]. Then for any generalized inverse <math>A^g</math>, there exist<ref name=":0" /> matrices <math>X</math>, <math>Y</math>, and <math>Z</math> such that

<math display="block">A^g = V \begin{bmatrix} \Sigma_1^{-1} & X \\ Y & Z \end{bmatrix} U^\operatorname{T}.</math>

Conversely, any choice of <math>X</math>, <math>Y</math>, and <math>Z</math> for matrix of this form is a generalized inverse of <math>A</math>.<ref name=":0" /> The <math>\{1,2\}</math>-inverses are exactly those for which <math>Z = Y \Sigma_1 X</math>, the <math>\{1,3\}</math>-inverses are exactly those for which <math>X = 0</math>, and the <math>\{1,4\}</math>-inverses are exactly those for which <math>Y = 0</math>. In particular, the pseudoinverse is given by <math>X = Y = Z = 0</math>:

<math display="block">A^+ = V \begin{bmatrix} \Sigma_1^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} U^\operatorname{T}.</math>

== Transformation consistency properties ==
In practical applications it is necessary to identify the class of matrix transformations that must be preserved by a generalized inverse. For example, the Moore–Penrose inverse, <math>A^+,</math> satisfies the following definition of consistency with respect to transformations involving unitary matrices ''U'' and ''V'':

:<math>(UAV)^+ = V^* A^+ U^*</math>.

The Drazin inverse, <math> A^\mathrm{D}</math> satisfies the following definition of consistency with respect to similarity transformations involving a nonsingular matrix ''S'':

:<math>\left(SAS^{-1}\right)^\mathrm{D} = S A^\mathrm{D} S^{-1}</math>.

The unit-consistent (UC) inverse,<ref>{{harvnb|Uhlmann|2018}}</ref> <math>A^\mathrm{U},</math> satisfies the following definition of consistency with respect to transformations involving nonsingular diagonal matrices ''D'' and ''E'':

:<math>(DAE)^\mathrm{U} = E^{-1} A^\mathrm{U} D^{-1}</math>.

The fact that the Moore–Penrose inverse provides consistency with respect to rotations (which are orthonormal transformations) explains its widespread use in physics and other applications in which Euclidean distances must be preserved. The UC inverse, by contrast, is applicable when system behavior is expected to be invariant with respect to the choice of units on different state variables, e.g., miles versus kilometers.
